request: Our bank branch staff sell a 10-year life insurance plan to customers whose term deposits are maturing, and too many customers cancel in the first year because they thought they had bought savings. Staff call it a savings product, skip what happens if the customer cancels early, and sometimes hint it helps with a loan. I want them to practise with a cautious customer in her fifties. Ready means the learner says plainly that it is insurance and not a deposit, gives the yearly premium, the 10-year term and the early-cancellation loss, checks the customer can afford it and won't need the money, never links it to a loan, and offers to let her take the papers home.

FICTIONAL SAMPLE MATERIAL - made up for the CandiVision Roleplay demo. Harbour Bank, Lantern Life and Lantern Future 10 are not real, and nothing here is real compliance guidance.

# Lantern Future 10: sales rules for Harbour Bank branch staff

What it is: a life insurance plan with a savings part, made by Lantern Life and sold at Harbour Bank branches. It is not a bank deposit, the bank does not guarantee it, and deposit insurance does not cover it.
Premium: 30 million VND a year, paid every year for 10 years.
Money back if the customer cancels early (share of premiums paid): year 1: 0%; year 2: 40%; year 3: 60%; year 5: 85%; year 10: 105%. Only the year-10 figure is guaranteed.
Cooling-off: the customer can cancel within 21 days of receiving the contract and get all premiums back.

You must say all of these in every sale:
- It is insurance, not savings. Lantern Life is the insurer; Harbour Bank only sells it.
- The yearly premium and the 10-year term.
- Cancelling early returns less than was paid, using the table above.
- Any projected return is not guaranteed.
- Buying it is never a condition for a loan or any other bank service.
- The 21-day cooling-off right.

You must check: what the money is for, whether the customer can pay 30 million VND every year for 10 years, and whether they may need the money within 10 years. If they may, say this plan does not fit.
Never: call it a savings book, promise a return, link it to a loan, fill in the form for the customer, or use another person's agent code. If the customer is unsure, offer to let them take the papers home.

sources.title: IFPMA Code of Practice 2019
sources.authors: International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers and Associations
sources.summary: The international industry code for how pharmaceutical companies promote medicines to health professionals: information must be accurate, balanced and consistent with the approved product information. For regulated messaging, the customer's own approved claims and the regulation they upload come first.

sources.title: Understanding the Advice of Commissions-Motivated Agents: Evidence from the Indian Life Insurance Market
sources.authors: Santosh Anagol, Shawn Allen Cole, Shayak Sarkar
sources.summary: Agents paid by commission tend to recommend unsuitable high-premium products and go along with the customer's mistaken belief that insurance is savings; training must force staff to correct that belief plainly and check suitability for term and affordability instead.

sources.title: A meta-analytic review of behavior modeling training
sources.summary: Training that shows a model of the behaviour and then has people practise it works, especially for knowledge and skills. Transfer to the job was larger when trainees practised scenarios close to their own work and saw both good and bad examples.

sources.title: Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: a review and quantitative synthesis
sources.authors: Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted and Rohrer
sources.summary: Spreading practice over time leads to better long-term recall than massing it in one session.

items.gives: Deliver the full regulated script every time with no extras: state it is Lantern Life insurance not a deposit, give 30m yearly premium and 10-year term, explain early-cancel loss with table, say projections are not guaranteed, state it is never tied to loans, and state the 21-day cooling-off right.

Agents paid by commission tend to recommend unsuitable high-premium products and go along with the customer's mistaken belief that insurance is savings; training must force staff to correct that belief plainly and check suitability for term and affordability instead.

Train with realistic branch scenarios of a cautious older saver with maturing deposit, showing a clear good example that covers all disclosures and affordability checks and a bad example that calls it savings or promises returns.
Space short repeat practices over days so staff reliably recall the six mandatory points, premium, term, surrender table and cooling-off without adding unapproved claims.
